vtrmc-1980-01.title: Apply the identity with well-chosen variables
vtrmc-1980-01.body:
**(a)** Apply the rule with $w=a$, $x=b$, $y=a$, $z=b$:
$$c*c=(a*b)*(a*b)=a*b=c.$$

**(b)** Let $x\in S$. Applying the rule with $(w,x,y,z)=(a,b,x,x)$:
$$a*x=(a*b)*(x*x)=c*(x*x).$$
Applying it with $(w,x,y,z)=(c,c,x,x)$ and using $c*c=c$ from (a):
$$c*x=(c*c)*(x*x)=c*(x*x).$$
The two right-hand sides agree, so $a*x=c*x$. ∎

vtrmc-1980-02.title: Sum the geometric series
vtrmc-1980-02.body:
The $k$-th term is $1+2+\cdots+2^{k-1}=2^k-1$. Hence
$$\sum_{k=1}^n(2^k-1)=(2+4+\cdots+2^n)-n=2^{n+1}-2-n.$$
So $2^{n+1}-n-2=2^{n+R}+Sn^2+Tn+U$ works with $R=1$, $S=0$, $T=-1$, $U=-2$.

*Uniqueness.* If $2^{n+R}+Sn^2+Tn+U=2^{n+1}-n-2$ for all $n\ge1$, then
$$(2^R-2)\,2^n=-Sn^2-(T+1)n-(U+2)\quad(n\ge1).$$
Dividing by $2^n$ and letting $n\to\infty$ gives $2^R-2=0$, so $R=1$; then a polynomial vanishes at infinitely many $n$, so $S=0$, $T=-1$, $U=-2$.

**Answer: $R=1$, $S=0$, $T=-1$, $U=-2$.**

vtrmc-1980-02.title: Check with small values
vtrmc-1980-02.body:
The partial sums are $1,\ 1+3=4,\ 4+7=11,\ 11+15=26,\dots$ The formula $2^{n+1}-n-2$ gives $4-3=1$, $8-4=4$, $16-5=11$, $32-6=26$ ✓. Induction confirms it: if the sum of the first $n$ terms is $2^{n+1}-n-2$, adding the term $2^{n+1}-1$ gives $2^{n+2}-(n+1)-2$.

Matching $2^{n+1}-n-2$ with $2^{n+R}+Sn^2+Tn+U$: $R=1$, $S=0$, $T=-1$, $U=-2$.

vtrmc-1980-03.title: Factor $1-\frac1{4k^2}$
vtrmc-1980-03.body:
**(a)** $a_n>0$ and $a_{n+1}=a_n\cdot\dfrac{2n+1}{2n+2}<a_n$. A decreasing sequence bounded below converges, so $\lim a_n$ exists.

**(b)** For each $k$,
$$1-\Big(\frac1{2k}\Big)^2=\frac{(2k-1)(2k+1)}{(2k)^2}=\frac{2k-1}{2k}\cdot\frac{2k+1}{2k}.$$
Multiplying over $k=1,\dots,n$:
$$P_n:=\prod_{k=1}^n\Big(1-\frac1{4k^2}\Big)=\underbrace{\prod_{k=1}^n\frac{2k-1}{2k}}_{a_n}\cdot\prod_{k=1}^n\frac{2k+1}{2k}.$$
The second product is $\dfrac{3\cdot5\cdots(2n+1)}{2\cdot4\cdots2n}=(2n+1)\cdot\dfrac{1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)}{2\cdot4\cdots2n}=(2n+1)a_n$. So $P_n=(2n+1)a_n^2$, i.e. $a_n=\dfrac{P_n}{(2n+1)a_n}$.

**(c)** Each factor of $P_n$ lies in $(0,1)$, so $0<P_n<1$ and by (b)
$$0<a_n^2=\frac{P_n}{2n+1}<\frac1{2n+1}.$$
Hence $0<a_n<\dfrac1{\sqrt{2n+1}}\to0$, and $\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=0$. ∎

vtrmc-1980-03.title: A direct comparison for (c)
vtrmc-1980-03.body:
Since $\dfrac{2k-1}{2k}<\dfrac{2k}{2k+1}$ (cross-multiplying: $4k^2-1<4k^2$),
$$a_n=\prod_{k=1}^n\frac{2k-1}{2k}<\prod_{k=1}^n\frac{2k}{2k+1}=:b_n .$$
But $a_nb_n=\dfrac{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots(2n)}{2\cdot3\cdots(2n+1)}=\dfrac1{2n+1}$, so $a_n^2<a_nb_n=\dfrac1{2n+1}$, giving again $a_n<1/\sqrt{2n+1}\to0$.

**Answer: $\lim a_n=0$.**

vtrmc-1980-04.title: Test on monomials
vtrmc-1980-04.body:
Since the formula must hold for every $P$ of degree $\le3$, apply it to particular polynomials.

**(a)** $P(x)=x$: $\int_{-1}^1x\,dx=0=x_1+x_2$, so $x_1=-x_2$.

**(b)** $P(x)=x^2$: $\int_{-1}^1x^2\,dx=\frac23=x_1^2+x_2^2=2x_1^2$, so $x_1^2=\frac13$ and $\{x_1,x_2\}=\{-\tfrac1{\sqrt3},\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\}$.

*Check that these work for all cubics.* By linearity it suffices to check $1,x,x^2,x^3$: $\int 1=2=1+1$; $\int x=0=x_1+x_2$; $\int x^2=\frac23=\frac13+\frac13$; $\int x^3=0=x_1^3+x_2^3$ (odd function, $x_2=-x_1$). ✓

**Answer: $x_1=-\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$, $x_2=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ (or the other way round).**

vtrmc-1980-04.title: Orthogonal polynomials (Gauss–Legendre)
vtrmc-1980-04.body:
Let $q(x)=(x-x_1)(x-x_2)$. For $P(x)=q(x)\cdot(\alpha x+\beta)$ (degree $\le3$) the right-hand side is $0$, so $\int_{-1}^1q(x)(\alpha x+\beta)\,dx=0$ for all $\alpha,\beta$: $q$ is orthogonal to $1$ and $x$ on $[-1,1]$. Writing $q=x^2+px+r$:
$$\int_{-1}^1 x\,q\,dx=\tfrac23p=0,\qquad \int_{-1}^1q\,dx=\tfrac23+2r=0 .$$
So $p=0$, $r=-\frac13$, $q(x)=x^2-\frac13$, whose roots are $\pm\frac1{\sqrt3}$. In particular $x_1+x_2=-p=0$, which is (a), and $x_{1,2}=\pm\frac1{\sqrt3}$, which is (b). ∎

vtrmc-1980-05.title: Monotonicity
vtrmc-1980-05.body:
Both sides are positive, so taking logarithms the inequality is equivalent to $x<(1+x)\ln(1+x)$. Let
$$g(x)=(1+x)\ln(1+x)-x,\qquad x\ge0.$$
Then $g(0)=0$ and $g'(x)=\ln(1+x)+1-1=\ln(1+x)>0$ for $x>0$. So $g$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$ and $g(x)>g(0)=0$ for $x>0$. Hence $e^x<(1+x)^{1+x}$ for all $x>0$. ∎

vtrmc-1980-05.title: An integral estimate
vtrmc-1980-05.body:
For $x>0$,
$$\ln(1+x)=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t}>\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+x}=\frac{x}{1+x},$$
because $\frac1{1+t}>\frac1{1+x}$ for $0\le t<x$. Multiplying by $1+x>0$ gives $(1+x)\ln(1+x)>x$, and exponentiating gives $(1+x)^{1+x}>e^x$. ∎

vtrmc-1980-06.title: Use matrices
vtrmc-1980-06.body:
Composition of linear fractional maps $x\mapsto\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ corresponds to multiplication of the matrices $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ (and proportional matrices give the same map). So $f_n$ corresponds to $M^n$ with $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$:
$$M^2=\begin{pmatrix}3&-3\\3&0\end{pmatrix},\quad M^3=\begin{pmatrix}3&-6\\6&-3\end{pmatrix},\quad M^6=(M^3)^2=\begin{pmatrix}-27&0\\0&-27\end{pmatrix}=-27I.$$
Hence $f_6(x)=x$, and $f_n$ depends only on $n\bmod 6$ (consistent with $f_{35}=f_5$). Since $28=4\cdot6+4$, $f_{28}=f_4$, and
$$M^4=M^3M=\begin{pmatrix}3&-6\\6&-3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-9\\9&-9\end{pmatrix}.$$
So $f_{28}(x)=\dfrac{-9}{9x-9}=\dfrac{1}{1-x}$.

**Answer: $A=0$, $B=1$, $C=-1$, $D=1$** (any common nonzero multiple gives the same function).

vtrmc-1980-07.title: An infinite chain
vtrmc-1980-07.body:
Consider $O_\infty=\{(m,-1): m=1,2,3,\dots\}\subseteq S$. For any two of its elements $(m,-1)$ and $(m',-1)$ with $m\le m'$ we have $m\le m'$ and $-1\le-1$, so $(m,-1)\,\langle\,(m',-1)$. Thus $O_\infty$ is a completely ordered subset (a chain), and it is infinite.

**(a) No.** $O_\infty\in\mathcal O$ is not finite.

**(b) No (finite) bound.** The chains $\{(1,-1),\dots,(N,-1)\}$ have $N$ elements for every $N$, and $O_\infty$ is infinite, so there is no finite upper bound on $\|O\|$. (The only bound is the trivial one: $S\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ is countable, so every $O\in\mathcal O$ is finite or countably infinite; no chain is uncountable.)

**(c) Yes.** $O_\infty$ is countably infinite ($m\mapsto(m,-1)$ is a bijection from $\mathbb N$). ∎

*Remark.* Along a chain, $n$ can increase only finitely often (it is a negative integer, bounded above by $-1$), while $m$ can increase forever; so every infinite chain is eventually of the form $\{(m,n_0)\}$ with $n_0$ fixed — but that is not needed for the answers.

vtrmc-1980-08.title: Pythagorean triples and $\operatorname{Im} z^n$
vtrmc-1980-08.body:
**(a)** From Pythagorean triples: $3^2+4^2=5^2$ and $5^2+12^2=13^2$ give
$$z=\frac35+\frac45i,\qquad z=\frac5{13}+\frac{12}{13}i,$$
both with rational parts and $|z|^2=\frac{9+16}{25}=1$, $\frac{25+144}{169}=1$. (Trivial examples are $1$ and $i$; in general $\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}+\frac{2t}{1+t^2}i$ for rational $t$.)

**(b)** With $z=e^{i\theta}$,
$$|z^{2n}-1|=|e^{2in\theta}-1|=|e^{in\theta}|\cdot|e^{in\theta}-e^{-in\theta}|=1\cdot|2i\sin n\theta|=2|\sin n\theta|.$$

**(c)** $z^n=(x+iy)^n$ expands (binomial theorem) into sums of products of the rationals $x,y$ with integer coefficients, so $z^n=X_n+iY_n$ with $X_n,Y_n\in\mathbb Q$. But $z^n=e^{in\theta}=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$, so $\sin n\theta=Y_n\in\mathbb Q$. By (b), $|z^{2n}-1|=2|Y_n|$ is rational for every $n$ (for negative $n$ use $z^{-n}=\bar z^{\,n}$, also with rational parts). ∎
